method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.) 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)' (approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024), 24 claims; LICENCE: © 2023 American Academy of Ophthalmology, all rights reserved; AAO terms bar reproduction or loading into AI programs without permission (read at the PPP PDF front matter and https://www.aao.org/terms-of-service). S2: QUOTED from Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113) 'Infectious keratitis: A review' (published 2022), 12 claims; LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC9542356). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, an Australian narrative review (Cabrera-Aguas, Khoo and Watson, Clin Exp Ophthalmol 2022, CC BY 4.0, quoted), for Australian incidence, severity grading, culture practice, the Australian empiric regimen, Australian resistance data and surgical complications. S1 claims and anchors are unchanged. S2 is a review, not a guideline; its Australian regimen is cited by it from the Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, which were not read directly (licensed). Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S2 Table 1 row 1 (gram-positive vs gram-negative features, PCR sensitivity, fluoroquinolone monotherapy concentrations). S1 is not a PMC source and has no appended tables.

claims.claim: **Suspect it with** pain, redness, blurred vision, light sensitivity and discharge, plus corneal infiltrate or ulcer and inflammation in the anterior chamber.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Contact lenses are the top risk factor in the US, and sleeping in them (orthokeratology included) is a major one;** in much of the rest of the world, trauma leads.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Slit-lamp picture:** a suppurative stromal infiltrate (especially one over 1 mm) with blurred edges, surrounding oedema and white-cell infiltration, usually an epithelial defect, and often an anterior-chamber reaction.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Australian incidence is low by world standards:** about 6.6 per 100 000 in 2015, against 27.6 per 100 000 in the US (1999) and 40.3 in England (2006).
claims.source_text: In developed countries, the incidence has been reported at 27.6 per 100 000 years in the United States (US) in 1999, 40.3 per 100 000 in England in 2006, and 6.6 per 100 000 in Australia in 2015.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Grade severity by size and depth:** mild is under 2 mm and less than 20% (100 μm) deep; moderate is 2–5 mm, 20%–50% (100–275 μm) deep with dense infiltrate to mid-stroma; severe is 5 mm or more, over 50% (>275 μm) deep with infiltrate reaching deep stroma. Greater severity goes with poorer outcomes.
claims.source_text: Mild corneal ulcers are those <2 mm in size with the depth of the ulcer <20% or 100 μm corneal thickness. Superficial infiltrates near the ulcer may also be seen. Moderate corneal ulcers range between 2 and 5 mm in size, depth of 20%-50% (100-275 μm) of the cornea, with dense infiltrates extending to the mid stroma. Severe ulcers are ≥5 mm, with a depth of more than 50% (>275 μm) and dense infiltrates reaching the deep layers of the corneal stroma. Poor patient outcomes have been associated with increased severity.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Gram-positive or gram-negative? (S2 table):** gram-positive cocci give a localised round or oval ulcer with greyish-white stromal infiltrate, distinct borders and little surrounding haze; gram-negative bacilli run a rapid, inflammatory course with dense stromal suppuration, a hazy surrounding cornea and an immune ring.
claims.source_text: Gram‐positive cocci : localised round or oval corneal ulceration, greyish/white stromal infiltrates, distinct borders, minimal surrounding stromal haze. Gram‐negative bacilli : rapid, inflammatory course, dense stromal suppuration, hazy surrounding cornea, immune ring
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Give a topical antibiotic for any corneal abrasion in a contact-lens wearer or after trauma,** ideally within 24 hours, which has been shown to prevent ulceration; it covers fungal as well as bacterial infection. **Do not patch** a lens-related abrasion or fit a bandage lens.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most community-acquired cases (small, off-centre ulcers) settle on empiric treatment** without smears or cultures.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Take smears and cultures before starting antibiotics when:** the infiltrate is central and large (within 3 mm of the centre and 2 mm or more across), there are 2 or more adjacent lesions, the stroma is deeply involved or melting, the anterior chamber shows 1+ cells or more, the cornea has had surgery, features suggest fungus, Acanthamoeba or mycobacteria, or there are several infiltrates.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Appearance alone is unreliable:** shown photographs, 15 cornea specialists told bacterial from fungal keratitis correctly in less than 70% of cases.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Scrape under proparacaine 0.5%, not tetracaine,** because tetracaine has antimicrobial activity.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A hypopyon in bacterial keratitis is usually sterile;** do not tap the aqueous or vitreous unless endophthalmitis is strongly suspected (after intraocular surgery, penetrating trauma or sepsis).
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **S2 prefers to culture every corneal ulcer before antibiotics start where possible,** a broader rule than S1's selective indications above.
claims.source_text: Preferably, all corneal ulcers should be cultured for the identification of the causal organism and the antibiotic susceptibility before commencing antimicrobial therapy.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Scraping in practice (S2):** let the media (two blood agars, chocolate agar, Sabouraud's slope, cooked meat medium) warm from the fridge for 1 h; after an anaesthetic drop (lignocaine 1% in S2), scrape the infiltrate with a blade or 25-gauge needle, putting the first samples on slides for staining and then onto the media.
claims.source_text: The culture media (two blood agars, chocolate agar, Sabouraud's agar slope and cooked meat medium) should be taken from the fridge and left for 1 h to reach room temperature. The corneal ulcer samples are then collected from the area of corneal infiltration using blades or typically 25‐gauge needles after instilling an anaesthetic eye drop (i.e., lignocaine 1%), with the first samples placed on glass slides for staining and then onto the media for culture.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Expect modest yields:** Gram stain shows the organism type in 60%–75% of bacterial cases, and scrapes grow an organism in 38% to 66%. For progressive disease, negative scrapes, or an organism that does not fit the picture, a corneal biopsy can be done.
claims.source_text: Gram staining detects the type of organism in 60%-75% of bacterial cases. … The positive culture rate from corneal scrapes ranges from 38% to 66%, from different studies worldwide., In cases of progressive BK or where a negative result has been obtained from corneal scrapes or the organism identified does not match the clinical picture, a corneal biopsy can be performed.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **PCR sensitivity for bacterial keratitis is 25%–88%** (S2 table), against 60%–75% for Gram staining and 38%–66% for culture.
claims.source_text: Gram staining : Sensitivity:60%-75% Culture : Sensitivity:38%-66% PCR : Sensitivity:25%-88%
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Antibiotic drops are the treatment of choice,** reaching high tissue levels. Ointments penetrate the cornea poorly, so keep them for bedtime in milder cases or as an add-on.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Central or severe keratitis** (deep stroma, or infiltrate over 2 mm with heavy suppuration): **load with drops every 5 to 15 minutes, then give them about hourly.**
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A single fluoroquinolone works as well as a fortified combination.** Consider fortified antibiotics for large or sight-threatening infiltrates, particularly with a hypopyon, and for eyes not responding.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Ciprofloxacin 0.3%, ofloxacin 0.3% and levofloxacin 1.5% are the FDA-approved agents;** fourth-generation fluoroquinolones are widely used off-label.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Fluoroquinolone resistance is rising.** Risks include recent fluoroquinolone use, hospital admission, age and recent eye surgery. They work poorly against MRSA, which is generally sensitive to vancomycin.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A cycloplegic can ease pain and reduce synechiae** from anterior-segment inflammation.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Systemic antibiotics are seldom needed,** except where infection spreads to the sclera or the cornea is perforating; they are mandatory for gonococcal keratitis.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Australian empiric regimen (as S2 reports current Australian guidance): ciprofloxacin 0.3% or ofloxacin 0.3%, or fortified cephazolin 5% plus gentamicin 0.9%, one drop every hour including overnight.**
claims.source_text: The current guidelines in Australia recommend empiric therapy with fluoroquinolones; 0.3% ciprofloxacin or 0.3% ofloxacin, or fortified combination therapy with 5% cephazolin plus 0.9% gentamicin; either treatment with one drop every hour including overnight.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Tailor treatment to culture and sensitivities. Be careful with fortified drops in ocular surface disease:** their toxicity has been reported as five times that of ofloxacin alone, and outcomes were poorer with fortified combinations than with ofloxacin.
claims.source_text: Treatment should be modified based on the results of culture and susceptibility testing. In patients with a history of OSD, care should be taken when prescribing fortified antibiotics to these patients, as fortified antibiotics have been reported to have drug toxicity five times greater than ofloxacin alone. Furthermore, poorer patient outcomes have been reported in OSD patients who were prescribed combination fortified antibiotics when compared with ofloxacin alone.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Fluoroquinolone resistance is lower in Australia:** the Australian Bacterial Ocular Surveillance System found ciprofloxacin resistance in 16% of S. aureus and 6% of coagulase-negative staphylococci, against 32.2% for each in the US ARMOUR data for 2009 to 2018, where 34.9% of S. aureus were MRSA.
claims.source_text: The Antibiotic Resistance Monitoring in Ocular Microorganisms (ARMOUR) cumulative report from 2009 to 2018 reported that 34.9% of S. aureus were methicillin‐resistant S. aureus (MRSA). Resistance to ciprofloxacin was 32.2% among all S. aureus (10.4% for Methicillin‐sensitive S. aureus and 72.7% for MRSA) and 32.2% for CoNS. … On the other hand, in Australia, the Bacterial Ocular Surveillance System reported lower rates of resistance to ciprofloxacin with 16% among all isolates of S. aureus and 6% of CoNS.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Fluoroquinolone monotherapy options (S2 table):** ofloxacin 0.3%, ciprofloxacin 0.3%, moxifloxacin 5 mg/ml or levofloxacin 15 mg/ml, chosen by local availability and surveillance data.
claims.source_text: Monotherapy with fluoroquinolones a … a Ofloxacin 0.3%, ciprofloxacin 0.3%, moxifloxacin 5 mg/ml or levofloxacin 15 mg/ml depending on local availability and surveillance data.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Adjunctive steroid is optional, not routine.** SCUT found no overall benefit from prednisolone phosphate 1% with antibiotics (and no extra harm); subgroups hinted at benefit for Pseudomonas, severe ulcers, and when started within 2 to 3 days of antibiotics.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Never add a steroid for Nocardia, fungus or Acanthamoeba.** Where the central cornea is involved, a steroid may be added after at least 2 to 3 days of steady improvement on antibiotics, usually once the organism is known and fungus excluded. Check IOP and review within 1 to 2 days of starting it.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If the patient is already on steroid drops at presentation, cut back or stop them until the infection is controlled;** warn that inflammation may flare briefly as they come off.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **See severe cases daily at first,** until they are stable or clearly improving.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Judge treatment by the clinical response.** Change the regimen if the eye has not improved or stabilised within 48 hours, but expect Pseudomonas and other gram-negative infections to look more inflamed for the first 24 to 48 hours despite correct therapy.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Poor response, especially with negative cultures, calls for reculture or biopsy;** stopping antibiotics for 12 to 24 hours beforehand may raise the yield. Drug toxicity or steroid withdrawal can mimic treatment failure.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Admit when the keratitis is severe or threatens sight, adherence is unlikely, or pain is severe,** and for patients who cannot instil drops at home.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Counsel lens wearers:** microbial keratitis affects up to 20 per 10,000 extended-wear users a year against 1 to 2 per 10,000 daily-wear users. Reassess lens type and wear before resuming, and consider daily disposables.
claims.locator: American Academy of Ophthalmology PPP Cornea/External Disease Committee (Rhee MK et al.), 'Bacterial Keratitis Preferred Practice Pattern (2023)', approved 22 September 2023; published February 2024, https://www.aao.org/education/preferred-practice-pattern/bacterial-keratitis-ppp-2023, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Progressive thinning, descemetocele or perforation needs surgery.** Cyanoacrylate glue is first line for a perforation (success 29% to 86%; often reapplied within a month); amniotic membrane is an alternative; therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty is the main option for rapidly progressing infection or a large perforation, though graft survival is roughly halved at 4 years in inflamed or steroid-treated eyes.
claims.source_text: Surgical interventions are indicated in severe lesions that present progressive stromal thinning, descemetocele formation and local perforation. The application of cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive is the first line intervention for corneal perforation providing a successful tectonic support for a short time, although requiring reapplication with a month after first application., The success of this adhesive ranges between 29% and 86% depending on the cause of the perforation, indications for applications and definition of success. Complications associated with its application include increased ocular inflammation, corneal neovascularisation and giant papillary conjunctivitis as well as long‐term adhesion., Another alternative is amniotic membrane transplantation which has anti‐inflammatory effects to accelerate corneal healing. However, a therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty (PK) remains the major intervention for the management of rapidly progressing infections and in large corneal perforations. Although it is usually a successful intervention, the probability of graft survival is reduced in about a half, at 4 years post‐intervention, in eyes with inflammation or with corticosteroid use at the time of graft.
claims.locator: Cabrera-Aguas M, Khoo P, Watson SL (Save Sight Institute, University of Sydney / Sydney Eye Hospital), Clinical & Experimental Ophthalmology 50(5):543 (doi 10.1111/ceo.14113), 'Infectious keratitis: A review', published 2022, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9542356/, retrieved 2026-09-24
